synopsis: Riemann-1.0 learns action prediction and visual dynamics in one transformer, ordering actions before their consequences. Robot deployment uses actual camera feedback; a second operating mode generates action-conditioned video. Pretraining moves from human-video pseudo actions through mixed trajectories to robot-only supervision. Strong reported task results accompany qualitative simulator examples, but no controlled ablation separates the effects of architecture, curriculum, and data scale. [E03, E04, E07, E08, E09, E11, E13, E16, E17]

problem.text: How can heterogeneous human videos, handheld demonstrations, and robot trajectories train executable control and visual dynamics together? The sources differ in control semantics, temporal density, and label reliability. The authors propose a common trajectory interface and causal action-before-observation modeling.

contributions.text: One shared transformer supports history-conditioned actions and action-conditioned future visuals through embodiment-specific control interfaces.
Progressive pretraining increases action supervision fidelity and its loss weight, aiming to transfer human interaction experience into executable robot control.
Physical execution, held-out instructions, three simulation benchmarks, and generated videos test distinct capabilities; their outcomes should remain separate.

inputs: Task instruction, embodiment identity, and camera-view configuration
Packed multi-view observations and externally supplied robot states
Historical actions; candidate future action chunks in visual-simulation mode
During pretraining, video-derived latent actions or embodiment-specific trajectory labels
outputs: Continuous action chunks in the selected embodiment's control representation
Action-conditioned visual latents, decoded into RGB observations in simulator mode

steps.name: Standardize embodied experience
steps.detail: Section 2.1 reports 230K+ hours overall: 200K+ human, 12K+ handheld/wearable, and 20K+ robot hours. Semantic segmentation, MANO hand reconstruction, camera-pose estimation, calibration, filtering, and semantic-aware sampling produce aligned trajectories. Embodiment-specific normalization preserves distinct physical control spaces.

steps.name: Encode observations and control
steps.detail: T5 encodes task, embodiment, and camera-view prompts. The Wan VAE and 3D patch embedding encode a packed multi-view canvas. Embodiment IDs select state/action projections and action heads around a shared transformer; visual prediction uses a shared latent head.

steps.name: Prevent unavailable future information
steps.detail: Teacher-forced clean history and noisy flow targets occupy one sequence. Structured visibility blocks future clean information while allowing attention within local generation blocks. Action chunks align to visual transitions. Validity masks exclude padding and invalid targets; padded channels remain zero during noise injection.

training.text: Stage I trains then freezes a latent-action VAE. Adjacent-frame transitions pass through a 32-dimensional bottleneck under reconstruction and weak KL losses; deterministic posterior means supply pseudo actions. With λ=0.1, WAM learns dynamics associations, not a deployable policy.
Stage II uses UMI, robot, and reconstructed human-hand trajectories with λ=0.5. Stage III retains only high-quality robot demonstrations with λ=0.9. Visual supervision remains active throughout.

Post-training jointly fits one generalist to four real-world tasks with λ=0.95. Section 4.2 gives three teleoperation hours per task; Section 5.1.1 gives 15 demonstrations per task without reconciling the descriptions.

inference.text: Initialize a KV cache with prompt, observation latent, and state. Denoise Gaussian action noise, cache and execute the chunk for apf low-level steps, then append real observations and final state. This policy loop does not require future-video generation.

Simulator mode conditions the latent head on policy, candidate-plan, or recorded actions and feeds predicted visuals back into history. States remain observed or replayed rather than generated, limiting its interpretation as an autonomous physical-state simulator.
When the fixed cache window fills, history resets around the latest observation. Window length and reset effects are unreported. Simulation benchmarks use 16 low-level action steps per visual latent.

equations.explanation: Equation (1): c is the task condition, z a visual latent, s an externally supplied robot state, a an action chunk, and T the rollout horizon. The visual factor receives the current action; the action factor receives only preceding history. No state-transition distribution is learned.

The flow path mixes data x with Gaussian noise ε at noise level σ. Latent and action heads regress velocity ε−x through squared errors under their respective causal conditions. Equation (4) weights these losses by λ; masks normalize over valid targets.

results.setting: Tianji Marvin dual-arm robot; joint post-training on ordered cube stacking, kitchen organization, clothes folding, and desk organization.
results.metric: Average final-task SR and milestone-based PSR (%)
results.comparison: G0.5: 70.00% SR, 80.18% PSR; SR gain 15.00 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Physical execution results. Main-suite trial counts and uncertainty are absent.

results.setting: Post-trained physical utensil storage, plate placement, and bowl stacking.
results.comparison: Best competing SR: G0.5, 35.0%; best competing PSR: LingBot-VLA, 80.2%.
results.interpretation: The strongest comparator differs by metric; this large advantage is task-specific.

results.setting: Seen object categories, held-out instructions; 10 robot trials per task.
results.interpretation: Transfer degrades with stricter instructions; four added requirements change together.

results.setting: Scenes, objects, and goals absent from real-world post-training; no additional demonstrations or updates; 10 trials per task.
results.value: Rubik’s cube to storage box 10/10; towel to basin 7/10; average 85.0%.
results.interpretation: Exclusion from the much larger pretraining corpus is not established.

results.setting: 300-task pretraining followed by Target-50 fine-tuning; evaluation on 50 target tasks.
results.comparison: ABot-M0.5: 70.6/44.3/45.6; average 54.2. Average gain: 8.4 percentage points.
results.interpretation: Largest gains concern composite groups within this adaptation protocol; not an independently established zero-shot evaluation.

results.setting: 50 bimanual tasks; 50 clean plus 500 randomized training demonstrations per task.
results.metric: Clean, Randomized, and average simulation SR (%)
results.interpretation: The average lead coexists with a 0.2-point deficit under randomization; uncertainty is unreported.

results.setting: Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites; 10 tasks per suite, 50 demonstrations per task.
results.interpretation: The 0.1-point average lead lacks uncertainty estimates; Riemann does not lead every suite.

limitations.text: No controlled ablation isolates causal ordering, visual loss, LAM, curriculum stages, or balancing. Architecture, data, and schedule effects remain confounded.

Figure 10 supplies qualitative simulator examples, without prediction-error metrics, counterfactual action tests, or measured planning benefits. Generated images do not establish physical execution success.
PSR is defined through intermediate milestones, but the scoring rubric is not reconstructable. Main-task trial counts and uncertainty are absent; held-out tasks have ten trials each.
Matched pretraining data and compute across baselines are not established. DreamZero* is the authors’ 5B reproduction, not an untouched official checkpoint or Riemann’s parameter count.

reproduction.text: Reconstruction requires the curated data manifest, semantic sampling weights, embodiment mappings/statistics, camera packing, temporal alignment, validity masks, and source-specific filtering settings. The paper describes their roles but not a fully executable recipe.

Model size, optimizer, batch size, training steps/compute, denoising budget, latency, cache length, and LAM KL coefficient remain unspecified. The paper identifies a frozen LAM annotator, but does not establish T5/Wan VAE freezing or detailed initialization.

Reader-proposed checks: compare matched-budget ordering variants on executed SR and latency; test visual predictions against changed-action replay controls. The illustrated edition specifies controls and falsifiable observations.

reasoning.text: One Model is supported by the shared transformer, despite specialized heads and a separate training-time LAM. Other mechanisms/Outside quadrants fits action-first autoregression: it does not extract actions by inverse dynamics from imagined futures or require simultaneous action–future denoising. Alignment follows from staged supervision; memory support is narrower, through cached history and long tasks without a memory ablation.

discussionQuestions: Does visual supervision improve executed policy success without test-time video generation? [E06, E07]
How should future states be supplied for genuinely counterfactual visual simulation? [E03, E16]
Which long-horizon tasks require history lost during cache resets? [E07, E11]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author block, and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The title page reads Riemann-1.0: An Embodied World Action Model for Physical AI; arXiv:2608.27033v1 [cs.RO], 27 Aug 2026. Its 16 named authors match the catalog in order. The displayed affiliation is Riemann Dynamics.

The corpus includes 200K+ hours of human video, 12K+ handheld/wearable hours, and 20K+ robot hours. Processing standardizes action-level trajectories using semantic annotation, hand/camera reconstruction, alignment, normalization, validity masks, filtering, and semantic-aware sampling.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 7–8, Section 3.2, Equation (1) and adjacent paragraphs
evidence.detail: The action conditional precedes the visual conditional, which additionally receives the current action. States are externally observed or replayed, not generated. Policy mode uses actual observations; simulator mode recursively uses predicted visual latents.

evidence.location: PDF p. 8, Figure 4; pp. 8–9, Section 3.2, input conditioning and embodiment-specific interfaces
evidence.detail: T5 encodes structured prompts; Wan VAE and 3D patch embedding encode packed views. Embodiment IDs select state/action projections and action heads around one shared Action/Video DiT backbone, with a shared latent velocity head.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Figure 5 and token alignment; p. 10, Section 3.2, causal attention and loss masking
evidence.detail: Clean history and noisy targets share a sequence. Action chunks align with latent transitions; attention excludes unavailable future clean tokens. Validity masks remove padded or invalid targets, and inactive padded channels remain zero during noise injection.

evidence.location: PDF p. 7, flow-matching preliminary; p. 10, Equations (2)–(4)
evidence.detail: The noise interpolation has target velocity ε−x. Separate latent and action velocity losses use their respective causal histories and combine as (1−λ)L_z+λL_a.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 3.2, Autoregressive online inference and Figure 6
evidence.detail: The cache starts from text, initial observation, and state. A denoised action chunk executes for apf steps; actual observations and state update the cache. A full cache resets around the latest observation.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–13, Sections 4 and 4.1, Stage I, Figure 7, and LAM objective
evidence.detail: A separately trained, frozen latent-action VAE supplies posterior-mean pseudo actions from adjacent frames through a 32-dimensional bottleneck. Stage I groups these into chunks and uses λ=0.1; the text explicitly excludes deployable-policy learning as its purpose.

evidence.location: PDF p. 12, Figure 7; p. 13, Section 4.1, Stage II and Stage III
evidence.detail: Stage II combines UMI, robot, and annotated human-hand trajectories with λ=0.5. Stage III retains robot demonstrations only and raises λ to 0.9 while preserving visual supervision.

Post-training combines four tasks into one generalist model with action weight 0.95. Section 4.2 gives three hours per task; Section 5.1.1 gives 15 demonstrations per task and identifies the Tianji Marvin dual-arm robot.

evidence.location: PDF p. 14, baseline setup; p. 15, Table 1 (all task/average SR and PSR columns, caption) and Section 5.1.2
evidence.detail: Table 1 reports Riemann task SR/PSR pairs 85.0/91.6, 90.0/98.4, 85.0/92.5, 80.0/95.2, averaging 85.00/94.43. G0.5 averages 70.00/80.18, ties folding SR 85.0 and desk SR 80.0; its kitchen SR is 35.0. LingBot-VLA kitchen PSR is 80.2. SR measures final completion; PSR measures milestone progress. DreamZero* is the authors’ 5B reproduction.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 15 and 17–18, Section 5.1.3 and Table 2
evidence.detail: Table 2 gives Riemann 8/10 and 5/10 compositional successes (65.0% average), then 10/10 and 7/10 OOD successes (85.0% average); overall 75.0%. π0.5 averages 45.0/50.0/47.5 and LingBot-VA 15.0/30.0/22.5, respectively. Color, receptacle, and order requirements change together. OOD exclusion concerns real-world post-training; no additional demonstrations or updates are used. Figure 9 says basket for the Rubik’s-cube example, while Table 2 and prose say storage box.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Section 5.2 temporal interface, Section 5.2.1, and Table 3 (all category and Average columns)
evidence.detail: Simulation uses 16 low-level steps per latent. RoboCasa uses 300-task pretraining then Target-50 fine-tuning. Riemann reports Atomic-Seen/Composite-Seen/Composite-Unseen 74.2/56.0/56.3 and average 62.6; ABot-M0.5 reports 70.6/44.3/45.6 and average 54.2. Composite gains are 11.7 and 10.7 percentage points.

evidence.location: PDF p. 18, Section 5.2.2; p. 19, Table 4, Riemann and ABot-M0.5 rows, Clean/Randomized/Average columns
evidence.detail: RoboTwin training covers 50 tasks with 50 clean plus 500 randomized demonstrations per task. Visually inspected Table 4 gives Riemann 94.6/94.0/94.3 and ABot-M0.5 94.0/94.2/94.1 for Clean/Randomized/Average, respectively.

evidence.location: PDF p. 19, Table 5 (all suites and Average column), Section 5.2.3
evidence.detail: LIBERO uses four suites with 10 tasks and 50 demonstrations per task. Riemann reports Spatial/Object/Goal/Long 99.6/100.0/97.6/98.6, average 99.0. Being-H0.5 and G0.5 average 98.9. Being-H0.5 Goal is 99.4 and G0.5 Long is 98.6, so Riemann does not strictly lead every suite.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 20–21, Figure 10 and complete Section 5.3
evidence.detail: Provided, policy-generated, or recorded actions condition visual-latent denoising; predicted or observed visuals can extend autoregressive history. Figure 10 illustrates heterogeneous embodiments. Section 5.3 supplies no quantitative visual-fidelity metric, changed-action control, or measured planning benefit.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 8–13, implementation/training descriptions; pp. 14–21, complete experiment Sections 5.1–5.3; p. 22, conclusion
evidence.detail: The method and training sections report interfaces and stage weights but omit Riemann parameter count, detailed optimizer/compute settings, LAM KL coefficient, denoising budget, and cache length. Experiments comprise task comparisons and qualitative rollouts, with no controlled mechanism ablation, inference timing, uncertainty estimates, or main four-task evaluation trial counts. No separate limitations section follows before References.

evidence.location: PDF p. 20, Figure 10, header and first three rows: Agibot G1, BaiHu GR2, Galbot Yinhe
evidence.detail: The figure labels uniformly sampled generated rollouts: Agibot G1 folding blue shorts, BaiHu GR2 picking up a carrot, and Galbot Yinhe folding and organizing clothes. The rows show successive generated camera frames; no ground-truth comparison or numeric action trajectory is displayed.
